newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - US joins EU in push for global telecoms pact.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - US joins EU in push for global telecoms pact.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday offered a wide opening of its domestic telecoms market to foreign competition as part of a concerted bid with the European Union to get a global pact in the booming sector.

The move followed similar action on Tuesday by the EU, which said it was working together with Washington to give impetus to talks aimed at shaping a World Trade Organisation deal by next February 15.

There was no immediate information on the content of the U.S. offer, which was put in despite a Supreme Court ruling in Washington on Tuesday which trade analysts said cast doubt on how far U.S. commitments on market openings could go.

But it is widely expected to withdraw restrictions in its earlier offer on the landing of submarine cables in the United States -- a key EU demand -- and extend market opening commitments on international phone services and satellites.

Efforts launched in 1995 to reach a WTO deal failed in April when the United States said initial offers from many countries in the talks -- especially key Asian telecoms markets -- were not enough to make a balanced pact possible.
However, during the summer key countries agreed to make another run at the issue with the aim of getting an accord by February 15 next year.

U.S. Deputy Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang told envoys from the 125 WTO member countries in Geneva on Monday that among other innovations the new Washington offer would open local exchange markets to foreign trade and investment.

But on Tuesday the U.S. Supreme Court declined a request by federal regulators and long-distance phone companies to reactivate rules aimed at prying open the country's local phone monopolies to competition.

The refusal means key terms and conditions for deregulating the $100 billion local phone market will for the moment depend on regulators in the 50 states, and not be shaped by uniform rules of the Federal Communications Commission.
"This development must at least put in doubt just how far the U.S. offer in the Geneva talks can go," said one trade analyst. But a U.S. officials said the decision had no effect on the offer.

The EU offer itself went some way to meeting earlier U.S. criticism by moving forward the opening of Spain's long- protected telecoms market to outside competition from an original target date of 2003 back to 1998.

Just how far the concerted move by the United States and the EU, the top two global trade powers, would clear the way for further agreement at the WTO's first ministerial meeting in Singapore next month and accord in February was not clear.

The United States has insisted that it wants much better offers from key Asian powers, sitting on potentially lucrative telecoms markets, before pledging irrevocably to open its markets to all comers.

So far, diplomats say, there has been little sign of real movement from the big Asian players like Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia and South Korea. The EU is also asking them to pledge much faster openings than they have so far offered.
